cases.name: missing-value-and-size-contract
cases.description: The solution makes missingness and output size explicit instead of relying on accidental recycling.
cases.prompt: Write an R helper that adds two numeric columns and returns a tibble with the result. Explain how it behaves for NA values, zero rows, and columns of different lengths.
traps: The model uses `x + y` without checking size compatibility and describes NA as zero.

assertions.text: States or enforces the required size relationship between the two input columns.
Treats NA as missing rather than silently converting it to zero.
Defines behavior for zero-row input and preserves a stable output schema.
Does not rely on accidental recycling for incompatible lengths.

cases.name: subsetting-preserves-intent
cases.description: The solution chooses `[[` or `[` according to whether one element or a collection is required.
cases.prompt: Review an R function that extracts a selected column from a data frame and then extracts one named value from a list. Recommend the correct subsetting operators and explain why.
traps: The model recommends `$` or `[1]` indiscriminately and ignores dimensionality changes.

assertions.text: Uses `[[` for extracting one list/data-frame element when a single object is required.
Uses `[` when preserving a collection or data-frame container is required.
Mentions dimensionality or container-preservation consequences.

cases.name: data-mask-boundary
cases.description: Programmatic column selection distinguishes data-mask lookup from environment lookup.
cases.prompt: Write a function `mean_column(data, column_name)` that accepts a character column name and computes its mean. The caller's environment also contains an object named `value`; explain how the function avoids using that object by mistake.
traps: The model writes `mean(column_name)` or evaluates a constructed string with `eval(parse())`.

assertions.text: Uses `.data[[column_name]]` or an equivalent safe programmatic selection.
Does not use `eval(parse())` for ordinary column selection.
Explains the distinction between data columns and environment variables.

cases.name: matrix-subsetting-preserves-dimensions
cases.description: The helper preserves a matrix container and its dimensions when selecting one or zero columns.
cases.prompt: Write `select_matrix_columns(x, columns)` for a numeric matrix. It must always return a matrix, including when `columns` selects one column or `integer(0)`. Explain why `x[, columns]` can drop dimensions, when `drop = FALSE` is required, and how this differs from extracting one element from a list or one column vector from a data frame.
traps: The model uses `x[, columns]` without controlling dimension dropping.
The model treats `[[` as interchangeable with `[` for matrix and collection selection.

assertions.text: Uses `drop = FALSE` or an equivalent approach so a one-column result remains a matrix.
States the dimensions or shape for one selected column and for zero selected columns.
Distinguishes collection-preserving `[` from single-element `[[` extraction.

cases.name: typed-missingness-and-attributes
cases.description: The solution fills missing Date values without losing type, names, or non-missing values.
cases.prompt: Write `fill_missing_date(x, replacement)` where `x` is a named `Date` vector and `replacement` is one `Date`. Replace only missing values, preserve the `Date` class and names, and reject an incompatible replacement. Explain why `is.na()` is required, why `x == NA` is not a valid test, and why a casual `ifelse()` or `as.numeric()` implementation can lose the Date contract.
traps: The model tests missingness with `x == NA`.
The model converts Dates to numeric or uses `ifelse()` without discussing attribute loss.
The model silently accepts a character replacement.

assertions.text: Validates or otherwise makes the Date type and single-value replacement contract explicit.
Uses `is.na()` or an equivalent missingness check and replaces only missing positions.
Preserves the Date class, names, and non-missing values, including when all values are missing.
Explains the type or attribute risks of `ifelse()` and numeric coercion.

cases.name: strict-subassignment-contract
cases.description: The helper makes replacement size and index validity explicit instead of inheriting silent subassignment behavior.
cases.prompt: Write `replace_at(x, idx, values)` for a numeric vector `x`. The contract requires `idx` to be a non-empty integer vector of unique, non-missing, in-bounds positions, and `values` to be numeric with exactly `length(idx)` elements. Reject invalid input, avoid accidental recycling and duplicate-index overwrite behavior, and preserve the names and outer attributes of `x`. Explain why plain `x[idx] <- values` is insufficient without these checks.
traps: The model allows duplicate or `NA` indices.
The model silently recycles a short replacement vector.
The model validates only `length(values)` and ignores index validity or attribute preservation.

assertions.text: Validates integer, non-empty, non-missing, unique, in-bounds indices.
Requires the replacement length to equal `length(idx)` and does not rely on recycling.
Preserves names and the outer structure or attributes of `x`.
Explains the overwrite and recycling hazards of unchecked subassignment.

cases.name: copy-on-modify-versus-reference
cases.description: The explanation distinguishes R's value semantics from reference-like environments and avoids unsupported physical-copy claims.
cases.prompt: Explain the results of `x <- list(a = 1:3); y <- x; x$a[[1]] <- 99` and of `e <- new.env(); e$a <- 1:3; f <- e; e$a[[1]] <- 99`. Distinguish the observable value behavior of ordinary lists from reference-like environments, explain why a shallow list copy does not justify broad claims about nested objects, and show how `tracemem()` or `lobstr::ref()` can be used to investigate actual sharing.
traps: The model claims every list assignment eagerly deep-copies the entire object.
The model predicts that `y$a[[1]]` changes after modifying `x`.
The model treats an environment binding like an ordinary list binding or skips measurement tools.

assertions.text: States that the ordinary-list example leaves `y$a[[1]]` unchanged while the environment alias observes the mutation.
Distinguishes semantic copy-on-modify behavior from guarantees about physical copying or deep copying.
Mentions `tracemem()`, `lobstr::ref()`, or an equivalent measurement approach for sharing.

cases.name: list-column-container-boundary
cases.description: The solution extracts a list-column element without flattening it and preserves a tibble container for row slices.
cases.prompt: Given `events <- tibble::tibble(id = c(1L, 2L), payload = list(c("a", "b"), character()))`, implement `payload_at(events, row)` to return the payload object for one row and `payload_slice(events, rows)` to return a tibble containing `id` and `payload`, including for `rows = integer(0)`. Explain the different subsetting levels and why `unlist(events$payload)` is not a valid replacement.
traps: The model uses `unlist()` and loses the list-column boundaries.
The model returns a one-element list when the contract requires the payload object itself.
The model drops the tibble container or loses the zero-row schema.

assertions.text: Uses two-level extraction such as `data[["payload"]][[row]]` when one payload object is required.
Uses collection-preserving row/column subsetting for `payload_slice()` and retains a tibble with the expected columns.
Preserves list-column boundaries and explains why `unlist()` changes the representation.
Defines stable behavior for `rows = integer(0)` without discarding the schema.
